summary: Registers a Telephone Number Mapping (ENUM) service for presence, focusing on provisioning pres URIs in ENUM. This lets a phone number be mapped to a presence address.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3953 registers a new kind of ENUM service, called E2U+pres, for the 'pres' URI scheme. ENUM is the system that uses DNS records to turn a telephone number such as +12025332600 into a URI. This document says which URI scheme a presence record should carry, and explains how a watcher can use that URI to find a presence service both it and the person being watched can use.

questions: how does enum find presence information
subtitle: How a phone number in the DNS can point to the address where that person's presence can be checked.

tldr.problem: ENUM can translate a telephone number into a URI, but there was no registered ENUM service for the 'pres' URI scheme, so a number could not be advertised with a generic way to find out whether the person behind it is reachable.
tldr.mechanism: The document registers an enumservice named 'E2U+pres' with the URI scheme 'pres', and says that a NAPTR record using it should carry a pres URI, which a watcher resolves to find a presence service that both sides support.
tldr.outcome: The registration lets a number's NAPTR record point at a generic presence URI rather than at one particular presence protocol. RFC 3953 was later updated by RFC 6118.

today: RFC 3953 was published in January 2005 as a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 6118. The registration it adds is the part of ENUM that maps a telephone number to a generic presence URI.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
ENUM (E.164 Number Mapping, described in RFC 3761) is a system that uses DNS (Domain Name Service, described in RFC 1034) to translate telephone numbers, such as +12025332600, into URIs (Uniform Resource Identifiers, described in RFC 2396), such as pres:user@host.com. ENUM exists primarily to make it easier to connect systems that rely on telephone numbers with systems that use URIs to identify resources.

Presence is a service defined in RFC 2778 that lets users of a communications service watch one another's availability and disposition in order to decide how to communicate. Presence information is highly dynamic. It generally says whether a user is online or offline, busy or idle, away from communications devices or nearby, and so on.

The IETF has defined a generic URI for identifying a presence service for a particular resource: the 'pres' URI scheme, defined in the Common Profile for Presence. This document describes an enumservice for advertising presence information associated with an E.164 number.
sections.plainLanguage: ENUM uses DNS records to turn a phone number into an address that software can use. Presence is a service that shows whether a person is free to talk. This document adds a way for a phone number to carry a generic address for checking that person's presence.

sections.title: Presence for E.164 Numbers
sections.content:
The document specifies an enumservice field that allows presence information to be provided for an E.164 number. This may include presence states associated with telephones, or the presence of non-telephony communications services advertised by ENUM.

Endpoints that take part in a presence architecture are known, following the framework in RFC 2778, as watchers and presentities. Watchers subscribe to the presence of presentities and are notified when that presence changes. Watchers generally monitor the presence of a group of presentities with whom they have an ongoing association.

The example given is a telephony service. Most cellular telephones today have an address book-like feature, a small database of names and telephone numbers. Such a telephone might act as a watcher, subscribing to the presence of some or all of the telephone numbers in its address book. When a presence-enabled telephone number is selected, the display could show its user the availability of the destination, and the user might then change their calling habits to match the availability of their associates.

The presence information that is shared varies by communications service. The IETF has defined a Presence Information Data Format (PIDF) for describing the presence data associated with a presentity. The baseline PIDF specification declares only two presence states, OPEN and CLOSED, where OPEN suggests the destination resource is able to accept communication requests and CLOSED that it is not. These two states give useful but rudimentary insight into the communications status of a presentity. PIDF is therefore extensible, and new sorts of statuses can be defined for specific communications services, for example a status corresponding to 'busy' for a telephony-based presence service. Extending PIDF for telephony services is, however, outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: One side watches, the other side is watched. A watcher subscribes to a presentity and is told when its state changes. The baseline format for that state has just two values, OPEN and CLOSED, though it can be extended with more detailed ones.

sections.title: The E2U+pres Enumservice
sections.content:
Traditionally the services field of a NAPTR record, as defined in RFC 3403, contains a string composed of two subfields: a 'protocol' subfield and a 'resolution service' subfield. ENUM in particular defines an 'E2U' (E.164 to URI) resolution service. This document defines an 'E2U+pres' enumservice for presence.

The scheme of the URI that appears in the regexp field of a NAPTR record using the 'E2U+pres' enumservice SHOULD be the 'pres' URI scheme. Other URI schemes appropriate to presence services MAY be used, but using the 'pres' URI scheme ensures a greater level of compatibility than using any URI specific to a particular presence protocol. The purpose of a pres URI is to provide a generic way to locate a presence service. Techniques for dereferencing the pres URI to locate a presence service are given in RFC 3861.

The 'pres' URI scheme does not identify any particular protocol that will be used to handle presence operations such as subscriptions and notifications. Rather, the mechanism in RFC 3861 details a way to discover whether the presence protocols supported by the watcher are also supported by the presentity. SIP is one protocol that can be used to convey presence information and manage subscriptions and notifications.
sections.plainLanguage: A NAPTR record for the number should carry a pres URI. That URI does not say which protocol to use; it is a generic pointer, and looking it up tells you which presence protocols both ends share.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DNS does not make policy decisions about the records it shares with an inquirer. All DNS records must be assumed to be available to all inquirers at all times. The information provided within an ENUM record set must therefore be considered open to the public, which is a cause for some privacy concerns.

Revealing a pres URI in itself is unlikely to introduce many privacy concerns, although, depending on the structure of the URI, it might reveal the full name or employer of the target. The use of anonymous URIs mitigates this risk. More serious privacy concerns are associated with the unauthorized distribution of presence information. For this reason, presence protocols have a number of security requirements, detailed in RFC 2779, that call for authentication of watchers, integrity and confidentiality properties, and similar measures to prevent abuse of presence information. Any presence protocol used in conjunction with the 'pres' URI scheme is required to meet these requirements.

Unlike a traditional telephone number, the resource identified by a pres URI may require that callers provide cryptographic credentials for authentication and authorization before presence information is returned. In concert with presence protocols, ENUM can therefore provide far greater protection from unwanted callers than the existing Public Switched Telephone Network does, despite the public availability of ENUM records.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can read DNS, so the ENUM record itself is public. The protection comes later: the presence service can demand credentials before it tells anyone anything.

sections.title: IANA Considerations and the Registration
sections.content: The document registers the 'E2U+pres' enumservice under the enumservice registry described in the IANA considerations in RFC 3761. The registration details are given in section 2, using the template defined in RFC 3761: the service name is "E2U+pres", the URI scheme is "pres:", the functional specification is in section 4, the security considerations are in section 6, the intended usage is COMMON, and the author is Jon Peterson of NeuStar.
sections.plainLanguage: This document's main act is to add one entry to the IANA registry of ENUM services, so that the name E2U+pres means a fixed thing for anyone using it.
